title: Spring Lecture #3: Master Apache Maven in one video

questions.question: What is the difference between a Maven dependency and a Maven plugin?
options: A dependency is downloaded from Maven Central, while a plugin is always written inside the project
A dependency runs during the build, while a plugin is a library your code imports
A dependency is a library your application code uses; a plugin is a tool Maven uses to perform build tasks
There is no difference; both terms describe JAR files listed under `<dependencies>`
questions.explanation: Dependencies (like `mysql-connector-j` or `hibernate-core`) are libraries used by your code. Plugins are used by Maven itself to compile, run tests, create JARs or run a Spring Boot app - e.g. `spring-boot-maven-plugin`. The second option swaps the two roles, and plugins are also downloaded from repositories rather than written in the project.

questions.question: A teammate accidentally deletes the `target` folder of a Maven project and panics. What should you tell them?
options: No problem: `target` is generated build output, and Maven recreates it on the next build
The Java source files were inside `target`, so they must be restored from Git
The `pom.xml` lived inside `target`, so the project can no longer be built
All downloaded dependencies were stored in `target`, so they are permanently lost
questions.explanation: `target` holds generated output: compiled `.class` files, test reports and the final JAR/WAR. Source code lives in `src/main/java`, `pom.xml` sits at the project root, and downloaded dependencies are cached in `~/.m2/repository`, so deleting `target` loses nothing that a build cannot recreate (`mvn clean` deletes it on purpose).

questions.question: A `pom.xml` has no `<packaging>` tag at all. What type of artifact does Maven build?
options: A WAR file
A POM-only artifact
Nothing, the build fails until packaging is declared
A JAR file
questions.explanation: If packaging is not specified, Maven defaults to `jar`. `war` must be declared explicitly for traditional web applications, and `pom` is used for parent/aggregator projects. The tag is optional, so the build does not fail.

questions.question: You run `mvn package` on the lecture's MavenDemo project (relevant part of the POM below). Where is the resulting artifact?
options: target/org.example.MavenDemo.jar
target/MavenDemo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
~/.m2/repository/org/example/MavenDemo/1.0-SNAPSHOT/MavenDemo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar only
target/classes/Main.jar
questions.explanation: The `package` phase creates the JAR inside `target`, named `artifactId-version.jar` by default. Copying it into `~/.m2/repository/org/example/MavenDemo/1.0-SNAPSHOT/` is what the later `install` phase does, which `mvn package` does not reach. The `groupId` is used for the repository folder path, not the JAR's file name.
questions.source: code: MavenDemo/pom.xml; notes p26, 28; excalidraw p3

questions.question: The MavenDemo POM declares only `mysql-connector-j` and `hibernate-core`, yet the IDE's External Libraries list shows many more JARs. Why?
options: Maven also downloads the dependencies of those dependencies (transitive dependencies)
The IDE adds every JAR found in Maven Central so code completion works
`<scope>compile</scope>` tells Maven to download all available versions of each library
Maven bundles the JDK's own classes as separate JAR dependencies
questions.explanation: If your project needs A, and A needs B, and B needs C, Maven reads their POMs and fetches B and C automatically. Hibernate in particular needs several supporting libraries. This is one of the biggest reasons Maven exists - without it you would have to find each of those JARs by hand.

questions.question: You run `mvn package`, but one unit test in `src/test/java` fails. What is the outcome?
options: The JAR is created anyway, because `package` only packages and does not run tests
Only the failing test class is left out of the JAR
The build fails at the `test` phase, so no new JAR is produced
Maven skips straight to `install` and stores the previous JAR in `.m2`
questions.explanation: Running a phase runs every earlier phase of that lifecycle first: validate -> compile -> test -> package. A failing test stops the build at the `test` phase, before packaging happens. This ordering is deliberate: it verifies the code works before the artifact is produced.

questions.question: This POM is built on a machine where `jackson-databind` 2.17.0 is not yet in `~/.m2/repository`. What does Maven do?
options: It fails immediately, because only artifacts in the local repository can be used offline-first
It downloads the JAR into the project's `target` folder and deletes it after the build
It searches only `company-repo`, because declaring a repository disables Maven Central
It checks the local repository, then the remote repositories, downloads the JAR and POM into `~/.m2/repository`, and reuses them in later builds
questions.explanation: Maven always checks the local repository first; if the artifact is missing it looks in the remote repositories (here the company repo and, by default, Maven Central), downloads the JAR and POM, caches them in `~/.m2/repository`, and uses them. That caching is why the first build is slower than later ones. Declaring an extra repository adds to the search, it does not remove Central.

questions.question: In the Spring Boot project from Lecture 2, the starter dependency has no `<version>` and builds fine. A student copies the same block into the plain MavenDemo POM (which has no `<parent>`), and the build fails with "dependencies.dependency.version ... is missing". Why?
questions.codeSnippet:
<!-- Lecture 2 project: works -->
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.0.6</version>
</parent>
...
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- MavenDemo project (no parent): fails -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
</dependency>
options: Starter dependencies can only be downloaded through Spring Initializr, not through Maven
In the Lecture 2 project the version is inherited from the parent POM's configuration; without a parent, Maven has no version and needs one stated explicitly
Maven always picks the latest version automatically, so the error must come from a missing `<scope>`
The `groupId` must be changed to `org.example` to match the MavenDemo project
questions.explanation: A dependency is identified by groupId + artifactId + version. In the Spring Boot project, `spring-boot-starter-parent` supplies managed versions, so the child POM may omit `<version>`. MavenDemo has no such parent configuration, so the version is missing and must be written explicitly - Maven never silently picks "the latest".
questions.source: notes p11, 15-16; code: Lecture 02 pom.xml, MavenDemo/pom.xml

questions.question: Your Wi-Fi dropped while Maven was downloading `hibernate-core`. Since then, every build fails with errors about a corrupted/invalid JAR, even though the POM is correct and you are back online. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Run `mvn clean`, because the corrupted JAR is stored in the `target` folder
Change the version in the POM to 6.x, because the current version is broken on Maven Central
Delete the `org/hibernate/orm/hibernate-core` folder inside `~/.m2/repository` and build again so Maven re-downloads it
Delete `settings.xml`, because it caches downloaded JARs
questions.explanation: Maven checks the local repository first, so a partially downloaded JAR cached in `.m2/repository` keeps being reused. Deleting that dependency's folder forces a fresh download; deleting the whole `.m2/repository` also works but re-downloads everything. `mvn clean` only removes `target`, and `settings.xml` holds user settings (credentials, proxies, mirrors), not cached JARs.

questions.question: On your laptop you have two Maven projects: a library `com.coderarmy:calculator-lib:1.0.0` and an app that declares it as a dependency. The app's build fails with "Could not find artifact com.coderarmy:calculator-lib:jar:1.0.0". Neither project is published anywhere. What is the simplest fix?
options: Run `mvn package` in the library, because the app reads JARs from the library's `target` folder
Push the library's source code to GitHub, because Maven downloads dependencies from Git repositories
Run `mvn site` in the library, so its documentation tells Maven where the JAR is
Run `mvn install` in the library, so its JAR is stored in the local `~/.m2/repository` where the app's build can find it
questions.explanation: `install` runs the lifecycle up to packaging and then copies the artifact into the local `.m2` repository, which is exactly where other local projects look first. `package` leaves the JAR only in the library's own `target` folder, which other projects do not search. GitHub stores source code, not Maven artifacts; sharing with other machines would need `deploy` to a remote repository.
